lessons.title: What Is a Blockchain?
Nodes, Blocks & Block Explorers

slots.practicalActivity: Watch both lessons, then open a real public block explorer (e.g. etherscan.io or mempool.space) and locate: the latest block, its block number and timestamp, the list of transactions inside it, and the node/network it belongs to. Click into one real transaction and identify its hash, sender, and receiver.
slots.deliverable: A short written note identifying the block number, block hash, and one transaction hash you found while exploring a real block explorer, with one sentence each on what a node, a block, and a block explorer do.

lessons.title: Hashing & Cryptographic Security
Consensus: Proof of Work vs. Proof of Stake
Blockchain in the Real World

slots.practicalActivity: Use a free online SHA-256 hash generator to hash the same short sentence twice and confirm the output is identical, then change a single character and confirm the hash changes completely. Write down which consensus mechanism (Proof of Work or Proof of Stake) Ethereum uses today and one real non-cryptocurrency use case from the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A short note recording the two SHA-256 hash outputs (identical input vs. one-character-changed input) plus one sentence naming Ethereum's current consensus mechanism and one real-world non-crypto blockchain use case.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review for Blockchain Foundations: without new instruction, pick one real cryptocurrency's block explorer (Bitcoin or Ethereum) and trace one full transaction from submission to confirmation, noting the block it landed in, its confirmation count, and any fee paid. Compare that to the proof-of-work vs. proof-of-stake distinction from the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A short write-up tracing one real transaction end to end on a public block explorer, naming its block, confirmation count, and fee, plus one paragraph explaining whether that chain uses Proof of Work or Proof of Stake.

lessons.title: What Is Cryptography?
Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Encryption
Digital Signatures & Public Key Cryptography

slots.practicalActivity: Generate a real public/private key pair (e.g. with an offline tool such as OpenSSL, or a reputable browser-based demo), encrypt a short message with the public key, and decrypt it with the private key. Then sign a short message with the private key and verify the signature with the public key, matching the symmetric-vs-asymmetric and digital-signature concepts from the lessons.
slots.deliverable: A short note recording the message you encrypted/decrypted and the one you signed/verified, plus one sentence explaining why asymmetric encryption, not symmetric, is what makes a digital signature possible.

slots.practicalActivity: Practice session: encrypt the same short message symmetrically (e.g. a simple AES tool) and then asymmetrically (using the key pair generated in the previous slot), and compare how key distribution differs between the two - who needs which key, and when a wrong key fails.
slots.deliverable: A short note recording both the symmetric and asymmetric encryption results for the same message, with one paragraph comparing their key-management differences.

lessons.title: Signing & Verifying Blockchain Transactions
PGP: Public Key Cryptography in the Real World

slots.practicalActivity: Find one real signed Bitcoin or Ethereum transaction on a public block explorer and identify the signature-related fields it exposes (sender address, signature/raw transaction data). Separately, look up a real public figure or project's published PGP public key (many open-source maintainers publish these) and read through its key fingerprint format.
slots.deliverable: A short note identifying one real on-chain transaction's sender address and signature-related field, plus the fingerprint of one real published PGP public key you looked up.

lessons.title: Precursors to Bitcoin: Bit Gold, e-gold & the Cypherpunks
The Bitcoin Whitepaper & the Genesis Block
Bitcoin Milestones: Pizza Day to Institutional Adoption

slots.practicalActivity: Read the real Bitcoin whitepaper (bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf) sections 1-3, then look up block 0 (the genesis block) on a Bitcoin block explorer and record its real block hash and timestamp. List two of the real historical milestones named in the lessons (e.g. Bitcoin Pizza Day, a halving date) in chronological order.
slots.deliverable: A short note with the genesis block's real hash and timestamp as found on a block explorer, plus a two-item timeline of real Bitcoin milestones from the lesson.

slots.practicalActivity: Find one real PGP-signed public message (many open-source project release announcements and security advisories are PGP-signed) and use a real verification tool to confirm the signature is valid against the publisher's published public key.
slots.deliverable: A short note identifying the real PGP-signed message found, the publisher's key fingerprint, and the verification tool's confirmation that the signature is valid.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review for Bitcoin Deep Dive: combine both practice sessions into one exercise - verify a real signed transaction's structure on a block explorer, then cross-reference the genesis block's timestamp against the whitepaper's publication date to confirm how much time passed between the two.
slots.deliverable: A short written timeline connecting the whitepaper's publication date, the genesis block's real on-chain timestamp, and one later milestone (e.g. a halving), with the transaction-signature fields noted from the earlier exercise.

lessons.title: What Is Ethereum? Smart Contracts & the EVM
Gas Fees on Ethereum

slots.practicalActivity: Install MetaMask as a browser extension, create a wallet, and switch it to the Sepolia test network. Find a real pending or recent transaction on Etherscan's Sepolia explorer and record its real gas price, gas used, and total fee paid, matching the gas-fee mechanics from the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A MetaMask wallet configured on Sepolia testnet, plus a short note recording one real Sepolia transaction's gas price, gas used, and total fee.

lessons.title: The History of Ethereum: Whitepaper to Frontier
The DAO Attack, the Merge & Ethereum Today

slots.practicalActivity: Request free Sepolia test ETH from a public faucet into the MetaMask wallet created in the previous slot. While waiting on the faucet, research the real DAO attack and the Merge (the real date Ethereum switched from Proof of Work to Proof of Stake) and write one paragraph on each, matching the lesson's history.
slots.deliverable: A MetaMask wallet funded with real Sepolia test ETH from a faucet, plus a two-paragraph note summarizing the real DAO attack and the real date/mechanics of the Merge.

slots.practicalActivity: Use the Sepolia test ETH funded in the previous slot to send a real test transaction from your MetaMask wallet to a second address you control (create a second MetaMask account for this). Watch it appear as pending, then confirmed, on Etherscan's Sepolia explorer, and record the real gas fee it cost.
slots.deliverable: A real, confirmed Sepolia test transaction between two of your own MetaMask addresses, with its Etherscan transaction hash and actual gas fee recorded.

slots.practicalActivity: Find a real verified contract on Etherscan (mainnet or Sepolia) and use its "Read Contract" tab to call a few view functions, then (if it's a Sepolia testnet contract you can safely interact with) use "Write Contract" connected to your MetaMask wallet to submit one real state-changing call, observing the gas cost.
slots.deliverable: A short note identifying the real contract address inspected, the view-function results read, and (if applicable) the transaction hash of one real write call submitted through Etherscan's Write Contract tab.

lessons.title: What Is Solidity? High-Level vs. Low-Level Languages
Why Solidity? Alternatives, the EVM & Compilation

slots.practicalActivity: Open the real Remix IDE (remix.ethereum.org) used throughout the course, create a new workspace, and create a blank .sol file. Compile an empty contract shell to confirm the Solidity compiler version selector and the Compile tab work, matching the compilation pipeline described in the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A new Remix workspace with one empty .sol file compiling successfully, plus a short note naming the compiler version selected and one reason (from the lesson) Solidity compiles down to EVM bytecode.

lessons.title: Solidity Dev Tools: Remix, Foundry & Hardhat
Contract Immutability, Gas & the ABI

slots.practicalActivity: In Remix, compile the empty contract from the previous slot and open the generated ABI (visible in the compiler's Compilation Details panel) and the bytecode. Identify the ABI's JSON structure and note that once deployed, a contract's code becomes immutable, matching the lesson's explanation of gas, the ABI, and immutability.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot or saved copy of the compiled contract's real ABI JSON from Remix, plus one sentence explaining why a deployed contract's code can never be changed afterward.

lessons.title: Your First Solidity Contract: Pragma, Contracts & Strings

slots.practicalActivity: In Remix, write the exact HelloWorld-style contract from the lesson: a pragma line, a contract declaration, and one string variable holding a greeting, plus a single-line and a multi-line comment. Compile it successfully.
slots.deliverable: A real .sol file in Remix containing a pragma statement, a named contract, one string state variable with an assigned value, and both comment styles, compiling with zero errors.

lessons.title: Compiling Your Contract & Viewing Bytecode
Deploying Your Contract to a Test Network

slots.practicalActivity: Compile the HelloWorld contract from the previous slot and inspect its real bytecode in Remix. Then deploy it to the Sepolia test network using Remix's "Injected Provider - MetaMask" environment and the wallet funded earlier, confirming the deployment transaction on Etherscan.
slots.deliverable: The HelloWorld contract's real deployed address on Sepolia, visible and verified on Etherscan, plus the raw bytecode viewed in Remix before deployment.

lessons.title: How the EVM Works: Stack, Opcodes & Gas
Writing Your First Function: setMessage

slots.practicalActivity: Add a real setMessage(string) function to the HelloWorld contract that updates the string state variable, redeploy it on the Remix JavaScript VM, and call setMessage twice with different values, confirming the stored value changes each time. Use Remix's debugger to step through the opcodes of one call.
slots.deliverable: An updated HelloWorld contract with a working setMessage function, called at least twice with different arguments and confirmed via the getter, plus a screenshot of the Remix debugger stepping through its opcodes.

lessons.title: Solidity Data Types: uint, int, bool & address

slots.practicalActivity: Extend the HelloWorld contract with one state variable of each real type covered in the lesson: a uint, an int, a bool, and an address, each with its own public getter. Deploy on the Remix JS VM and read back every value to confirm the defaults and types behave as taught.
slots.deliverable: A contract with working uint, int, bool, and address state variables, each deployed and read back correctly in Remix, with a short note on each type's real default value.

lessons.title: The Constructor: Initializing Your Contract
Reading vs. Writing State: the view Keyword

slots.practicalActivity: Add a constructor to the multi-type contract from the previous slot that sets the uint, bool, and address values at deploy time from constructor arguments, and add one view function that reads two of those values and returns a computed result without modifying state.
slots.deliverable: A contract whose constructor sets initial values from deploy-time arguments (confirmed by deploying it twice with different arguments) and one view function proven, via Remix's gas estimate, to cost zero gas when called.

lessons.title: Control Flow: if/else Statements & the Ternary Operator

slots.practicalActivity: Write a small contract function that takes a uint input and uses a real if/else chain to return one of three string outcomes depending on the value's range, then rewrite the same logic using the ternary operator for a simpler two-way case, exactly as shown in the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A deployed contract with one function using if/else and a second function using the ternary operator, both tested in Remix with at least three different input values each.

lessons.title: For & While Loops: continue and break

slots.practicalActivity: Write a function with a real for loop that sums the numbers 1 through a given input, a second function using a while loop that does the same, and a third loop that uses continue to skip even numbers and break once a running total exceeds a threshold, matching every pattern in the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A deployed contract with a for-loop sum function, a while-loop sum function, and a third function demonstrating both continue and break, each tested in Remix against at least two different inputs.

slots.practicalActivity: Practice session: write three new small functions from scratch (no new instruction) that combine this chapter's tools - one using a constructor plus a view function, one using if/else plus a loop, and one using a while loop with a break condition tied to a state variable.
slots.deliverable: Three additional working functions, each deployed and tested in Remix with at least two calls, demonstrating constructor+view, if/else+loop, and while+break combinations.

slots.practicalActivity: Practice session: build a small Profile contract from scratch (no new instruction) with a uint age, an address owner, and a bool isVerified field, a constructor that sets all three at deploy time, and a view function that returns a computed combination of them, reusing the data-types and constructor patterns from this chapter.
slots.deliverable: A deployed Profile contract with a constructor-initialized uint, address, and bool, plus a working view function, tested by deploying it twice with two different sets of constructor arguments.

slots.practicalActivity: Practice session: write a small access-gated function from scratch that uses if/else to check a caller's address against a stored owner address and returns a different string depending on the match, then rewrite the same check using the ternary operator, matching this chapter's control-flow tools.
slots.deliverable: A deployed contract with both an if/else version and a ternary-operator version of the same owner-check function, each tested from the owner account and from a second, non-owner account.

slots.practicalActivity: Practice session: write a new function from scratch that uses a for loop to find the maximum value in a fixed uint array, and a second function that uses a while loop with break to stop early once it finds a value above a given threshold, extending this chapter's loop patterns to a new problem.
slots.deliverable: A deployed contract with a working max-finder for loop function and a threshold-search while loop function using break, each tested against an array of at least five values.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone discussion: using Remix's debugger, step through the opcodes of two different functions built this chapter - one simple view function and one function containing a loop - and compare roughly how many more steps/how much more gas the looped function consumes.
slots.deliverable: A short written comparison of the two functions' opcode step counts and gas costs as observed in the Remix debugger, with one sentence explaining why the loop costs more.

slots.practicalActivity: Deploy the loop-based summing contract from the for/while-loops lesson to the Sepolia test network via MetaMask instead of the local JS VM, and call each function once as a real on-chain transaction, recording the actual gas cost of the loop versus the view function's free call.
slots.deliverable: The loop contract's real deployed address on Sepolia with at least one real on-chain transaction calling a loop function, plus a note comparing its gas cost to a free view-function call on the same contract.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review lab for Solidity Programming: without new instruction, build one original contract from scratch that combines a constructor, at least two data types, a view function, an if/else or ternary check, and a loop, solving one small coherent problem of your choosing (e.g. a simple savings tracker or a number-classifier contract).
slots.deliverable: One original contract combining a constructor, multiple data types, a view function, conditional logic, and a loop into a single coherent, successfully compiling and deployable program, with a short note on the problem it solves.

lessons.title: Mappings: Solidity's Key-Value Store

slots.practicalActivity: Write a contract with a real mapping(address => uint256) balances variable, a deposit() payable function that increases the caller's mapped balance, and a getBalance() view function, exactly matching the key-value pattern taught in the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A deployed contract with a working address-to-uint256 mapping, tested by depositing from at least two different Remix accounts and confirming each account's balance is tracked independently.

lessons.title: Arrays & Enums
Arrays in Practice: push, pop & removeAtIndex

slots.practicalActivity: Add a dynamic uint array and a real enum (e.g. a Status enum with at least three states) to a contract, then implement push, pop, and a removeAtIndex function exactly as taught, testing each against an array seeded with at least four values.
slots.deliverable: A deployed contract with a working dynamic array supporting push, pop, and removeAtIndex, plus a working enum variable, all tested in Remix with the array's contents verified before and after each operation.

lessons.title: Structs: Grouping Related Data
Function Modifiers: onlyOwner & Access Control

slots.practicalActivity: Define a struct grouping at least three related fields (e.g. a User struct with name, balance, and isActive), store several in an array or mapping, and add a real onlyOwner modifier restricting one function to the contract's deployer, matching the access-control pattern from the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A deployed contract with a working struct stored in a mapping or array, plus an onlyOwner-protected function proven to succeed from the owner account and revert from a second, non-owner Remix account.

lessons.title: Events: How Contracts Talk to the Outside World
A Simple Token Transfer Function

slots.practicalActivity: Add a real Transfer event to the mapping-based balance contract from earlier, emit it inside a new transfer(address to, uint256 amount) function that moves value between two mapped balances, and confirm the event shows up in Remix's transaction logs after calling it.
slots.deliverable: A deployed contract with a working transfer() function that emits a Transfer event, confirmed by inspecting the event log in Remix's transaction details after a real call between two accounts.

lessons.title: The ERC-20 Interface & Token Metadata
Implementing Transfer, Approve & TransferFrom

slots.practicalActivity: Start a new MyToken.sol contract implementing the real ERC-20 interface by hand: name, symbol, decimals, totalSupply, balanceOf, transfer, approve, and transferFrom, matching the interface and implementation shown in the lesson, with the allowance mapping used by approve/transferFrom.
slots.deliverable: A deployed hand-written ERC-20 token contract with working transfer, approve, and transferFrom functions, tested by approving a second Remix account and having it successfully call transferFrom on the first account's tokens.

lessons.title: Minting & Burning Your Own Tokens
Building an ERC-20 Token with OpenZeppelin

slots.practicalActivity: Add real mint() and burn() functions to the hand-written MyToken contract, increasing and decreasing totalSupply and a holder's balance. Then, in a separate file, build the same token using OpenZeppelin's ERC20 base contract (imported in Remix via GitHub path) and compare how much code each version required.
slots.deliverable: A hand-written token with working mint/burn functions, plus a second, separately deployed OpenZeppelin-based ERC-20 token, with a short written comparison of the two implementations' line counts and safety guarantees.

lessons.title: How Tokens Actually Get Bought and Sold
What Is ERC-721? Understanding NFTs

slots.practicalActivity: Look up one real liquidity pool or DEX listing for an actual ERC-20 token on a service like Etherscan or a DEX explorer to see how token trading works in practice. Then begin a new NFT.sol file declaring the real state an ERC-721 contract needs: a mapping from tokenId to owner and a mapping from tokenId to tokenURI, matching the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A short note identifying one real ERC-20 token's trading venue and liquidity as found on-chain, plus a started ERC-721 contract file with owner and tokenURI mappings declared and compiling.

lessons.title: Building an ERC-721 Contract: State, Events & Minting

slots.practicalActivity: Complete the ERC-721 contract from the previous slot: add the real Transfer event, an ownerOf() view function, and a mint() function that assigns a new tokenId to a given address and sets its tokenURI, exactly as built in the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A deployed ERC-721 contract with a working mint function, tested by minting at least two NFTs to two different addresses and confirming ownerOf() and tokenURI() return correctly for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Practice session: build a brand-new mapping-based ledger contract from scratch (no new instruction) that uses a struct to group each account's balance and active status, an event on every balance change, and an onlyOwner-protected admin function - combining this chapter's core tools into one original design.
slots.deliverable: One original contract combining a struct, a mapping, an event, and an onlyOwner modifier into a working ledger, deployed and tested in Remix with at least two accounts.

slots.practicalActivity: Deploy the ORIGINAL hand-written MyToken ERC-20 contract (not the OpenZeppelin version) to the Sepolia test network via MetaMask, verify its source code on Etherscan, and perform one real transfer and one real approve/transferFrom pair on-chain.
slots.deliverable: The hand-written MyToken contract's real, verified address on Sepolia Etherscan, with one confirmed transfer transaction and one confirmed transferFrom transaction visible on its page.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a minimal ERC-721 NFT contract a second time, this time inheriting from OpenZeppelin's ERC721 base contract instead of writing the owner/tokenURI mappings by hand, and compare how much custom code each version required.
slots.deliverable: A second, OpenZeppelin-based ERC-721 contract deployed and tested with the same mint/ownerOf/tokenURI scenarios used on the hand-written version, plus a short written comparison of the two implementations.

slots.practicalActivity: Rebuild the hand-written MyToken ERC-20 contract's mint/burn/approve logic as a fresh file, this time inheriting from OpenZeppelin's ERC20 and Ownable contracts instead of writing the allowance and ownership logic by hand, confirming the same behavior with far less custom code.
slots.deliverable: A second OpenZeppelin-based token contract with owner-restricted minting, deployed and tested with the same mint/transfer/approve scenarios used on the hand-written version, plus a one-paragraph note on what OpenZeppelin handled for you.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-paragraph security comparison of your hand-written ERC-20 contract versus the OpenZeppelin-based version, naming at least two specific safety guarantees OpenZeppelin's audited implementation provides that your hand-written version either lacks or had to reimplement yourself.
slots.deliverable: A short written comparison naming at least two concrete safety or correctness guarantees the OpenZeppelin ERC-20 implementation provides over the hand-written version.

slots.practicalActivity: Deploy both the OpenZeppelin ERC-20 token and the ERC-721 NFT contract to the Sepolia test network via MetaMask, mint one real NFT and transfer a real amount of the token on-chain, then verify both contracts' source code on Etherscan using the Verify & Publish tool.
slots.deliverable: Two real, verified contracts on Sepolia Etherscan (one ERC-20, one ERC-721), each with at least one real on-chain mint or transfer transaction linked from the contract page.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review lab for Token Standards: extend either the ERC-20 or ERC-721 contract from this chapter with one new feature not shown in class - for example a maximum supply cap on the token, or a maximum-mints-per-wallet limit on the NFT - and prove the new restriction is enforced.
slots.deliverable: An updated, redeployed token or NFT contract enforcing one new rule not covered in the lessons, proven by a Remix test that succeeds right up to the limit and reverts once it is exceeded.

lessons.title: Imports, Libraries & OpenZeppelin

slots.practicalActivity: Set up a real local project folder on your machine, initialize it with npm, and install OpenZeppelin Contracts as a real npm dependency. Import one real OpenZeppelin contract (e.g. ERC20.sol) by its node_modules path into a local .sol file and confirm it resolves, matching the import patterns from the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A real local npm project with OpenZeppelin Contracts installed as a dependency and one local Solidity file that successfully imports and compiles against it.

lessons.title: Command Line Basics: npm, git & the Terminal

slots.practicalActivity: In the local project folder from the previous slot, initialize a real git repository, make an initial commit, create a .gitignore excluding node_modules, and practice the core git commands from the lesson (status, add, commit, log) at least twice each.
slots.deliverable: A local git repository with a proper .gitignore and at least two real commits, plus a terminal log (git log output) showing both commits.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Foundry (or Hardhat, whichever the course tooling lesson referenced) into the local project from the previous two slots, scaffold its standard folder structure (src/test/script or contracts/test), and move one of your earlier Remix contracts (e.g. the MyToken ERC-20) into the project's source folder, confirming it compiles from the command line.
slots.deliverable: A working Foundry or Hardhat project with the standard scaffolded folders, containing one of your earlier contracts, confirmed to compile successfully via the command-line build command.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real automated test file for the MyToken contract inside the Foundry/Hardhat project, covering at least three cases: a successful transfer, a failed transfer from insufficient balance, and a successful approve/transferFrom pair. Run the test suite from the terminal and get all tests passing.
slots.deliverable: A real test file with at least three passing automated tests for the token contract, plus the terminal output showing the full test suite run and pass.

lessons.title: Building an Ether Wallet

slots.practicalActivity: Build the EtherWallet contract exactly as shown in the lesson: a payable deposit() (or receive()) function and a withdraw() function restricted to the contract's owner, deployed on the Remix JS VM.
slots.deliverable: A deployed EtherWallet contract tested by depositing real test ETH from one account and successfully withdrawing it as the owner, with a withdraw attempt from a non-owner account confirmed to revert.

lessons.title: The Multi-Signature Wallet: Setting Up Shared Control

slots.practicalActivity: Build the multi-signature wallet's state and constructor exactly as taught: an array of owner addresses, a required-confirmations count, and the submit/approve/revoke transaction-tracking structures, deployed with at least three owner addresses from Remix's account list.
slots.deliverable: A deployed multi-signature wallet contract initialized with three real owner addresses and a required-confirmation threshold, with its owners and threshold confirmed by calling the contract's public getters.

lessons.title: Building an English Auction for NFTs

slots.practicalActivity: Build the EnglishAuction contract's state, events, constructor, and start() function exactly as taught, referencing an existing IERC721 NFT contract - reuse the ERC-721 NFT contract built in the Token Standards chapter as the NFT it auctions.
slots.deliverable: A deployed EnglishAuction contract whose start() function successfully transfers a real NFT (from your earlier ERC-721 contract) into escrow, confirmed by calling ownerOf() on the NFT contract and seeing the auction contract listed as the new owner.

lessons.title: Bidding, Withdrawing & Preventing Reentrancy

slots.practicalActivity: Complete the EnglishAuction contract with bid(), withdraw(), and end() exactly as taught, then run a full auction from at least two different Remix accounts: two increasing bids, an outbid withdrawal, and a final end() that pays the seller and transfers the NFT to the winner.
slots.deliverable: A completed EnglishAuction contract proven end to end: two real bids from two accounts, one successful withdrawal by the outbid account, and a final end() call confirmed to transfer the NFT to the highest bidder and ETH to the seller.

slots.practicalActivity: Build and test the EtherWallet contract locally in Remix's JavaScript VM before touching testnet: deposit test ETH from two different accounts, confirm the owner can withdraw, and confirm a non-owner's withdraw attempt reverts.
slots.deliverable: A locally deployed EtherWallet contract tested with a deposit from two accounts, a successful owner withdrawal, and a confirmed revert on a non-owner withdrawal attempt, all on the Remix JS VM.

slots.practicalActivity: Build and test the multi-signature wallet locally in Remix's JS VM using at least three local accounts as owners: fund it, submit one transaction, approve it from a second owner account to meet the required-confirmation threshold, and execute it.
slots.deliverable: A locally deployed multi-signature wallet with three owner accounts, one transaction submitted, approved by a second owner, and successfully executed, all on the Remix JS VM before moving to testnet.

slots.practicalActivity: Build and test the completed EnglishAuction contract locally with at least two Remix accounts bidding against each other - two increasing bids, one outbid withdrawal, and a final end() - confirming the full cycle works on the JS VM before deploying it to testnet.
slots.deliverable: A locally deployed EnglishAuction contract proven end to end on the Remix JS VM with two competing bidders, one withdrawal, and a final end() transferring the NFT and paying the seller.

slots.practicalActivity: Before deploying any of this chapter's three DApps to testnet, write a short comparison of their real-world purposes - a personal wallet, a shared-control treasury, and a public marketplace mechanism - and the specific access-control or escrow pattern each one relies on.
slots.deliverable: A short written comparison of the EtherWallet, multi-signature wallet, and English Auction, naming each one's real-world purpose and its core access-control or escrow mechanism.

slots.practicalActivity: Deploy the EtherWallet contract from this chapter to the Sepolia test network via MetaMask, and perform a real deposit and a real owner withdrawal using actual test ETH, confirming both transactions on Etherscan.
slots.deliverable: The EtherWallet contract's real address on Sepolia Etherscan, with one confirmed deposit transaction and one confirmed owner-withdrawal transaction visible on its page.

slots.practicalActivity: Deploy the multi-signature wallet to Sepolia, fund it with real test ETH, and submit, approve, and execute one real transaction using at least two of its MetaMask-controlled owner accounts to meet the required-confirmation threshold.
slots.deliverable: The multi-signature wallet's real address on Sepolia with one submitted transaction confirmed by multiple owner accounts and successfully executed, visible as linked transactions on Etherscan.

slots.practicalActivity: Deploy the completed EnglishAuction contract to Sepolia alongside your existing ERC-721 NFT contract, and run one full real auction on-chain: start it, place two real bids from two MetaMask accounts, withdraw the outbid amount, and end it to transfer the NFT and pay the seller.
slots.deliverable: A fully completed, real on-chain English auction on Sepolia with every step (start, two bids, a withdrawal, and end) confirmed as separate transactions on Etherscan, and the NFT's new owner confirmed via ownerOf().

slots.practicalActivity: Review the EnglishAuction's withdraw() function for the same reentrancy risk covered later in the course, and add a nonReentrant-style guard (either hand-written or from OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard) before the external ETH transfer, redeploying and re-running the full auction to confirm it still behaves correctly.
slots.deliverable: An updated EnglishAuction contract with a reentrancy guard added to withdraw(), redeployed and re-tested with the same full auction cycle used in the previous slot, confirming identical correct behavior.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review lab for Full-Stack DApp Development: demo all three real DApp projects built this chapter - the EtherWallet, the multi-signature wallet, and the English Auction - back to back on Sepolia, narrating what each transaction does and why.
slots.deliverable: A short recorded or written walkthrough demoing the EtherWallet, multi-signature wallet, and English Auction all working end to end on Sepolia, each referencing its real Etherscan transaction history.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter capstone discussion: for each of the three DApps built this chapter, diagram (on paper or in a simple text outline) exactly which contract functions a real frontend built with ethers.js or web3.js would need to call, and in what order, to support a full user flow (deposit/withdraw, submit/approve/execute, bid/withdraw/end).
slots.deliverable: Three short function-call diagrams or outlines (one per DApp) mapping each real contract function to the step of a frontend user flow that would call it.

lessons.title: Understanding Reentrancy: The DAO Hack

slots.practicalActivity: Research the real 2016 DAO hack using at least one primary or reputable secondary source, and write a plain-language summary of how the attacker exploited the same reentrancy pattern explained in the lesson to drain funds before the balance was ever reset.
slots.deliverable: A short written summary of the real DAO hack, naming the vulnerable pattern (external call before state update) and roughly how much ETH was drained, in your own words.

lessons.title: Writing a Vulnerable Contract and Exploiting It

slots.practicalActivity: Build the exact vulnerable EtherStore contract and the Attack contract from the lesson in Remix's JS VM, deposit test ETH from two accounts, then call attack() and confirm the exploit really drains more ETH from EtherStore than the attacker ever deposited.
slots.deliverable: A real, working reentrancy exploit reproduced in Remix: EtherStore's balance driven to zero and the Attack contract's balance shown to exceed its original deposit, matching the lesson's live demonstration.

slots.practicalActivity: Before moving on, rebuild the exact vulnerable EtherStore contract from scratch in a fresh Remix file, from memory where possible, and manually underline or annotate the single line responsible for the bug before re-checking it against the lesson's version.
slots.deliverable: A freshly rebuilt EtherStore contract with the exact buggy line identified and annotated in your own words, compared afterward against the lesson's original.

slots.practicalActivity: Rebuild the exact Attack contract from scratch against your freshly rebuilt EtherStore, and run the real reentrancy exploit again end to end, confirming the same balance-draining result the lesson demonstrated live.
slots.deliverable: A freshly rebuilt Attack contract that successfully drains more ETH from your own freshly rebuilt EtherStore than was ever deposited, matching the lesson's live result.

lessons.title: Fixing Reentrancy: Checks-Effects-Interactions & the Guard Modifier

slots.practicalActivity: Fix the EtherStore contract from the previous slot using the real Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern (reset the balance before the external call) and add a nonReentrant guard modifier, then redeploy and re-run the exact same Attack contract to confirm the exploit now fails.
slots.deliverable: A fixed EtherStore contract where the same Attack contract that succeeded earlier now fails (reverts) on the reentrant call, proving both the CEI reorder and the guard modifier work.

slots.practicalActivity: Re-read the EtherStore contract's original withdraw() function line by line without looking at the fix, and write out, in your own words, the exact sequence of external calls between EtherStore and Attack that let the exploit drain more ETH than was deposited - before checking your explanation against the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A written, step-by-step trace (in your own words) of the reentrancy exploit's call sequence, written before re-checking the lesson, plus a note on anything you got wrong or missed.

slots.practicalActivity: Audit the EtherWallet contract built in the Full-Stack DApp Development chapter for the same reentrancy bug: identify whether its withdraw() function follows Checks-Effects-Interactions, and if it doesn't, fix it using the same pattern applied to EtherStore.
slots.deliverable: A short written audit note on the EtherWallet contract's withdraw() function, plus (if a fix was needed) an updated, redeployed version confirmed safe against the same Attack-contract pattern.

slots.practicalActivity: Audit the English Auction contract's withdraw() function from the DApp chapter for reentrancy exposure, confirming whether the guard added earlier is sufficient, and attempt to run the Attack-contract pattern against it to prove it holds up.
slots.deliverable: A short written audit note on the English Auction's withdraw() function confirming its reentrancy protection, backed by a real attempted exploit run in Remix that fails to drain funds.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short, plain-language security audit report covering every contract built across the course - the ERC-20 token, the ERC-721 NFT, the EtherWallet, the multi-signature wallet, and the English Auction - listing each one's reentrancy exposure and whether it has been fixed.
slots.deliverable: A one-to-two-page written security audit report listing all five course contracts, their reentrancy exposure status, and the fix applied (or confirmation that none was needed) for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Final capstone session 1: choose one contract from the course (the ERC-20 token, the ERC-721 NFT, the EtherWallet, the multi-signature wallet, or the English Auction) and deploy a fully-secured, final version of it to the Sepolia test network, incorporating every fix and best practice covered across the course.
slots.deliverable: One chosen contract's final, fully-secured version deployed as a real address on Sepolia, with its security fixes (access control, reentrancy guard, checks-effects-interactions) all present in the deployed code.

slots.practicalActivity: Final capstone session 2: verify the capstone contract's source code on Sepolia Etherscan using Verify & Publish, then write a short README documenting its public functions, constructor arguments, and the specific security review performed on it earlier in the chapter.
slots.deliverable: The capstone contract verified and publicly readable on Sepolia Etherscan, plus a README documenting its functions, constructor arguments, and security review.

slots.practicalActivity: Final capstone wrap-up: rehearse a 3-5 minute walkthrough demo of the finished, secured capstone contract - its purpose, its real Sepolia Etherscan link, the vulnerability it was audited against, and the fix applied - ready to present in a portfolio or technical interview.
slots.deliverable: A rehearsed, portfolio-ready demo script (written or recorded) walking through the capstone contract's purpose, its live Sepolia Etherscan link, and the specific security review and fix behind it.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After completing this course, a student can read and write real Solidity smart contracts, build and deploy ERC-20 tokens and ERC-721 NFTs, build full-stack DApps (wallets, a multi-signature wallet, and an NFT auction) on the Ethereum testnet, and identify, exploit, and fix a real reentrancy vulnerability like the one behind the DAO hack.
